scripts.full_script: I'm the only kid at superhero school with no super power, so I've been faking one for a year to impress my crush. Her power is floating, and she can't turn it off. She's tied to her desk by the ankle. For laser eyes, I used two flashlights. For flying, a leaf blower. For super strength, a cardboard car. If anyone found out I'd be kicked out, but weird things kept happening. Every time I sat next to her, she stopped floating. The whole class said she liked me, and whenever I walked past the fire kid, his flames went out. Then a villain who grows as big as a building smashed through the wall. Every hero bounced off him. He snapped her rope and grabbed her. I ran straight at him. The closer I got, the smaller he got. When I reached him, he was normal size. She dropped into my arms. That's when I got it. I do have a power. Every power near me stops working. So she never liked me. It was just my power. I asked her out anyway. She said yes. Then she cut the rope off her ankle. Next to you, I don't need it.

scripts.full_script: In this town, nothing grew on the hill, not grass, not weeds, nothing. Every seed anyone ever planted up there was dead in a week. So an eight-year-old Theo carried a tiny pine tree up that hill. The whole street laughed at him. Theo didn't argue. He just went home, got another seed, and planted that one too. That became his rule. Every time somebody laughed at him, he planted another tree. And the loudest laugh always came from Rosa, the girl next door. She laughed at every single one, always right when he was about to give up. At 12, Theo had 40 trees, and 39 of them were dead. But one was alive, nobody could explain it. Not even Theo. At 18, the whole school laughed when he skipped prom to carry buckets up the hill. That night, he planted six more. At 30, the town laughed when he spent his savings on baby trees. He planted every single one. Rosa laughed so hard she had to sit down. At 50, people stopped laughing. They just shook their heads. So he planted one for every head shake. And by 70, Theo's hill was the only green thing anyone could see from town. Then the storm came. It rained for three days straight. The river jumped the bridge. And on the third night, the hill above the town started to slide. Theo was up there alone, in the dark. Tying his youngest trees to six, so the water wouldn't rip them out. The mud was up to his knees. He slipped twice. He kept the time. Down below, everyone ran out into the street, staring up at that hill, waiting for the mud to come down on their houses. It never came. Thousands of roots were holding that hill together. The water just ran down slow and brown, between the trees and into the river. The next morning, the whole town climbed the hill. The same people who'd laughed at him for 60 years stood there in the mud and didn't say a word. Theo walked past all of them, up to the very first tree that ever lived. Leaning against it was an old rusty watering can. The same can that had been sitting there, full, every morning since he was 12. Scratched into the side was one word, Rosa.

scripts.full_script: In this world, everything is either blue or pink. Even the sky was painted in two halves. Every morning, I walked past blue houses, blue trees, and blue cars. Across the street, everything was pink, and nobody dared cross to the other side. Because above our city, hung a giant balance scale. Every person added weight to their color. And if either side touched the ground, that color would take over the entire world. That's why both sides were always fighting. Every day, giant blue and pink tanks attacked each other. And they didn't fire normal bullets, they fired color balloons. One pink splash could turn a blue person pink, and one blue splash could turn them right back. I was blue, just like Leo and Rose. We always stuck together, even during the biggest battles. Until one morning, a pink tank suddenly aimed straight at Leo. Leo, watch out! Before I could reach him, Rose pushed him away. Splash! Her entire body turned pink, and before we could save her, pink soldiers took her away. The next day, I spotted Rose inside a pink tank. Rose, it's me! But she aimed her cannon straight at us. Boom! A pink balloon exploded beside me. Three blue soldiers instantly turned pink. Leo grabbed my arm. We have to bring her back! So we stole the biggest blue tank in our city. I aimed directly at Rose. But then, hundreds of pink tanks surrounded us. They started firing from every direction. I fired back. Boom! Pink soldiers were turning blue everywhere. The giant scale began tilting toward our side. We were about to win. But suddenly, Rose aimed her cannon straight at me. I aimed mine back at her. Stop! Leo screamed, but it was too late. We both fired, and Leo jumped right between us. Boom! Both balloons hit him at the exact same time. Blue and pink exploded all over his body. I thought he'd turn blue, or maybe pink, but instead, he turned purple. Suddenly, the giant scale stopped moving. Crack! A third purple side appeared between blue and pink. Purple roads spread across our city. Purple houses rose from the ground. Even the sky split into three colors. And that's when I realized we had just created a third world. I was still blue. Rose was still pink, but Leo, he was the first person in the purple world. But the balance was still shaking. Leo needed more people on his side. Comment, Leo, to choose the purple side and save the world.

A prince tried a catapult. He landed in the next kingdom. A wizard tried flying. He forgot how to land. So I tried to. Her hair. A kite. A pole vault. I fell every time. But every time I fell a pillow landed under me first. She never threw one for anybody else. Then we heard the strongest knight in the land was coming on Sunday. He'd never fallen off anything in his life. On Saturday night I sat down by the tower and gave up. That's when I noticed the doormat. It said please knock. Every boy had wiped his feet on it. So I knocked. She opened the door right away. It had never been locked. We took the stairs.

scripts.full_script: A goddess got kicked out of Heaven. She can only go back when I become a good person. Heaven's list says I'm the worst kid in town. I once forgot to return a library book, so she moved into my room. She took my bed. I took the floor. She made me do my homework. It turned into a bird and flew away. She made me share my lunch with the bully. It exploded in his face. She sent me to bed early. I woke up the next afternoon. Every time I got in trouble, her halo glowed a little brighter and she smiled. She tried pizza for the first time. She ate eleven slices. She sat with me on the roof every night counting stars. I didn't want her to leave, but a goddess belongs in Heaven. So I tried my hardest. I helped every old lady cross the street. I gave my piggy bank to the dog shelter. That night I caught her turning my homework into a bird. She'd been doing it all along. She never wanted to go back. Heaven doesn't have pizza or me. Now I forget to return a library book every single week.

He beat me at every video game. At school, his sister never said one word to me. So I asked him about her every day. Every time he said the same thing. She likes you. Just ask her idiot. He always wore his cap pull down low. His voice was kind of high. He said it hadn't broken yet. He had the same red hair clip as her. He said he was holding it for her. He knew everything about her, even that I'm scared of geese. Every time I said her name, he dropped whatever he was holding. And I'd never seen them in the same room. So for my birthday, I invited them both. He showed up alone. He said he'd go get his sister and ran behind my house. A minute later, she walked out holding his cap. She doesn't have a twin brother. She'd been too shy to talk to me for a whole year. Then she looked at me and said, just ask me, idiot.

scripts.full_script: At my school, whatever your t-shirt says, you are. And at the last bell on the last day, it's forever. Turn it inside out, and it doesn't count. All he wore, I need a nap. He's been asleep since Tuesday. We flip his shirt for tests. Rocco borrowed his dad's world's best dad's shirt. He's nine. He has back pain. Our new principal, Mr. Pickett, never unbuttons his blazer. Nobody's ever seen his shirt. Me? Mine's plain blue. It doesn't say anything, so I'm just me. My best friend, Dante, wears stripes. He laughs at all my jokes, even the bad ones. On the last day, everybody wears plain shirts. Everybody. Then, Mr. Pickett handed out free spirit shirts. A big smiley face on the front. No words. 600 kids put them on. Mine wouldn't go over my crown. I never take it off. The words were on the back. I do what I'm told. You can't read your own back. Sit up straight, said Mr. Pickett. 600 kids sat up. Carry me. They lifted him over their heads. His blazer fell open. His t-shirt said, principal. He was only the principal because his shirt said so. All day, they did what he said. No recess, no lunch, extra math. I grabbed Dante's shirt to pull it off. Dante, said Mr. Pickett. So he did. 2.52. I told Dante my best joke. He didn't laugh. I just wanted to hear him laugh. Dante, I said, laugh. He laughed. I do what I'm told. It doesn't say who's telling. I ran for the stage. 2.59. I grabbed the microphone. Everybody. Turn every shirt in this gym inside out. 600 kids turned theirs. Then they turned to Mr. Pickett's. Stop, said Mr. Pickett. Nobody stopped. 3 o'clock. His shirt said nothing now. He was just some guy in a blazer. Dante laughed at my next joke. Nobody told him to.

scripts.full_script: In this world, you can only eat foods that start with the first letter of your name. And every mayor we've ever had has a name that starts with Pete. You see, Paul gets pizza, pancakes, and popcorn. Charlotte gets cake, cookies, and chocolate. Hazel gets hamburgers and hot dogs. Levi gets lasagna and lemonade. And everybody knows that if you take one bite of the wrong letter, you swell up like a giant balloon. So, in our town, every restaurant has 26 doors, one for each letter. Parents pick a baby's name by reading the menu first. School lunch takes two hours because the lunch lady cooks 26 different meals. Nobody has named a kid with an X in a hundred years. And on top of town hall, there's a huge net called the balloon catcher, just in case. My name is Ezra, and I've eaten eggs 3,000 days in a row. Eggs for breakfast, eggs for lunch, and eggplant for dinner. On my last birthday, my cake was a boiled egg with a candle in it. My best friend Hazel has the luckiest letter in school, and she eats her hamburgers right in front of me. My little sister, Ellie, is five, and eggs are the only thing she'll eat. Our mayor, Mayor Paul, decides what every food is called. Last year, when ice cream got popular, he changed its name to polar cream. And now only the pee people get it. Then, on Monday, he made a new law. By Friday, eggs would be called protein pearls. That night at dinner, Ellie pushed her eggplant away and didn't eat a thing. So I started looking around, and I noticed three things. One, in the town museum, the first law book is open under glass. The list for pee is three pages long. Every other letter gets three lines. Two, the balloon catcher is covered in spiderwebs. Nobody has ever used it, not once. And three, next to the law book, there's an old baby picture of our mayor. And the little sign under it says, baby Zachary Paul. And that's when I understood it. There was never any magic. The rule is just a law written by the very first mayor, Mayor Patricia. So her family could keep the best food and the mayor's chair forever. Nobody ever swelled up, because nobody ever dared to take a bite. And our mayor isn't even a pea. He's a Z, hiding behind his middle name. On Friday, the whole town was in the square. Mayor Paul sat at a long table full of pizza, pancakes, and pie, with his pen over the egg law. I walked right up to his table, picked up a slice of pizza, and took the biggest bite of my life. Hazel covered her eyes. Ellie held her breath. Everybody looked up at the balloon catcher. Nothing happened. So, Hazel grabbed a pancake. Ellie grabbed a slice of pie. Then, one by one, the whole town took a bite of a letter that wasn't theirs. That same afternoon, the town voted. The food law is gone for everyone, except for the one person who lied about his letter. Mayor Zachary has to follow it for the rest of his life. Zucchini for breakfast, zucchini for lunch, and zucchini for dinner. Ellie ate pie until she fell asleep, and I haven't touched an egg since. And now everyone in town eats whatever they want, except our old mayor, whose name starts with Z.

scripts.full_script: The armies of two kingdoms have fought for years over a tower of white iron. The priests say it fell from the sky. This morning, it started counting. Ten rings of light glow on its side, and one just went dark. Nobody on either side knows what happens when the last one does. Every dawn, ten thousand red shields and ten thousand blue shields meet at its feet. By sunset, we push them back ten steps. By the next sunset, they push us back, eleven. The blues say the tower is theirs because it leans toward them. We say it is ours because its door faces us. The priests say the gods inside will punish whoever lets go of it, so nobody lets go. The young learn to fight for it before they learn to read. At school, recess is shield wall practice, and homework is sharpening. The baker bakes for the army. The blacksmith makes nothing but swords. All of us spend our whole lives trying to take that tower. I was best in my class. Now I lead the red wall. Our shields are red, with eight corners, and one holy word no one can read. The priests say it means courage. After every battle, I carry the shields of the fallen to their doors myself. This morning, I knocked on four doors. Bram stands on my right. His shield has covered my sword arms since school. When the first ring went dark, something inside the tower started knocking. The priests said the gods were waking up angry. King Oswin had ten thousand ropes tied to it to pull it our way. When they wake, all of it will be mine. He said, lead them. I led them. At seven rings, we took the towers left foot. Nine shields for me to carry home. At five rings, the blues took it back. Thirty shields. One was going to the baker's door. Good said the king. Shields can be used again. At three rings, the blue army came with everything. Crash! Twenty thousand shields met under the tower. A blue sword came for my open side. Bram stepped out of the wall and took it on his shield. Keep going, Captain. He said he held the gap alone until the horns blew. He didn't get up. Nobody stands on my right now. One ring left. Both armies pulled back and the tower still wasn't ours. If it won't be mine, it won't be anywhere. Said King Oswin, he turned the catapults on it. Clang! The rock left a dent. Nobody throws rocks at a god. I ran to the tower with Bram's shield to beg the gods not to punish us. I cut the rope across the door and knocked three times. The door opened. A girl in white stood there. Behind her stood hundreds of people in white. Every one of them looked more afraid than I was. Storms don't knock three times. She said, forgive us. Don't let the gods punish us. What god? The ones in this tower. It's a rocket, a space rocket, and we're not gods. We're people. It fell from the sky. It has never left the ground. Our grandparents locked this door a hundred years ago. The day the world burned. The world didn't burn. I live in it. We were taught nothing with a lie out here. We were taught gods were alive in there. I held up Bram's shield. My friend fell under this today. It says courage. It says stop. It's a road sign. We learned that it's six. The gods will burn you for that. Nobody is burning anybody. We all had cities of glass. We could fly. Then came one war. Everyone who knew how things worked hit in here. Now you hit each other with road signs over the last ship. Wake up. Then why is it counting? It waited a hundred years for the world to heal. Today it leaves. To look for a world with people in it. There are people in this one. She looked past me at 20,000 shields. I can see that. Close the door. Set an old man behind her. That is not people. Nothing lives out there. They're alive. Close it. She stepped outside. The door closed behind her. We ran. The last ring went dark. The tower rose and 10,000 ropes snapped like thread. It left with everyone who knew everything. To look for us somewhere else.

scripts.full_script: My crush said she'd go out with whoever brought her the moon, so I built a rocket in my garage. I've liked her for years. She has no idea. She'd been crying all week. She must really want the moon. My first rocket was a lawn chair and a hundred fireworks. I landed in the principal's pool. My second was 2000 soda bottles. I landed on the school roof. Lost cat posters were all over town. I was too busy to read them. Every launch my mom packed me a tuna sandwich. Every landing it was gone. My third rocket was my dad's car. Don't tell him. It worked. I made it to the moon and grabbed a moon rock. I crashed, landed in her backyard right on her dad's barbecue. She ran out. I held up the rock. I brought you the moon. She didn't look at it. She was looking behind me. A cat in a tiny helmet climbed out of my rocket. It was her cat. His name is Moon. He'd been eating my tuna all week. She hugged Moon, then me. Oh and her dog is missing too. His name is Sun.

scripts.full_script: We only move when the eye blinks. Whoever moves while it's open turns to stone. We eat one bite per blink. A wedding lasts three blinks. A haircut lasts all year. This morning it stopped blinking. Nobody knows what it's looking at. The eye hangs over our city like a second moon. It blinks about every nine seconds. A blink is as long as a sneeze. That's when we live. Step freeze. Step freeze. We learn to talk without moving our lips before we learn to read. We sleep standing up, leaning on each other like books. Babies are born in a single blink. Don't ask. Our fastest runner has finished one race. It took him 19 days. And the streets are full of statues. Mr. Hale sneezed with the eye open. He's on third street, still sneezing. In winter, kids put a scarf on him. Mo is four. He lives next door. Four-year-olds can't hold still. So somebody has to hold them. I've held Mo still through about three million blinks. Every time the eye closes, he whispers, now I say, and he gets one wiggle. This morning I was turning around to grab him. The eye opened. It never closed. Everybody in the city is facing the eye. The way we always stop. It's polite. I'm facing the other way, with one arm out. Like I'm asking the hills to dance. Nine seconds. Nothing. An hour. Nothing. Miss Okoro was halfway into a chair. She has been sitting on air since breakfast. The baker is holding a hot tray. He's being very brave about it. Two people on Bell Street got married this morning. They're still on the kiss. Old Dez is stuck next to me, holding a ladder. Don't you twitch, kid. He said, with his lips shut. My arm hurts. Then let it hurt. Whispers crawled down the street with their lips shut. It's angry. It's sick. It's looking for somebody. By noon, my arm was shaking. Now? Mo whispered. Not yet. Then it started to rain. Out of a clear sky. A drop landed on my lip. Salt. Is he crying? Mo whispered. The eye was watering. It wasn't staring. It was trying not to blink. Why would anything try that hard not to blink? I'm the only one facing the hills. There are four hills behind our city. I've counted them my whole life. Today, there are five. The fifth one has a foot. The foot is lifted over our wall. Like somebody stopped in the middle of a step. It's as tall as the clouds. And it has too many elbows. It isn't stone. It's holding still. Same as us. It only moves when the eye is closed. Every morning of my life, the hills looked a little closer. We said the city was growing. One blink. One step. The eye was never watching us. We were just standing in front of the thing it was watching. It can't look at only one of us. So it stops everything it sees. We learn to live in the blinks. So did the thing behind us. I tried to say it without moving my lips. It's behind us. It came out as a hum. Mo Giggle only does hurt. What do you see kid? A hill with a foot. He was quiet for a long time. How close? One step. The rain is getting heavier. The lid has started to shake. Everybody I love is facing the wrong way. Mo whispers. Not now Mo, please. Not now. My whole life. I wished that thing would look away. Tonight, I'm begging it not to blink.

She said it was too late to cancel the sandwiches. So I went to my own funeral in a fake mustache and my grandpa's hat. My hair didn't fit under it. The bully cried the hardest. He said I was the only kid who never ran from him. I ran from him every day. The lunch lady cried into the meatloaf. My teacher said she loved my essays. She gave every one of them a seat. My best friend gave a speech. Then he asked if he could have my bite. Finally, my crush walked up. She never said a word to me. She said she'd like me since second grade. She said she'd been too scared to tell me, and now it was too late. I almost ripped off the mustache right there. After the funeral, she walked straight up to me. She'd spotted my green spikes the second I walked in. Then she smiled. Nice mustache, seer.

scripts.full_script: A witch turned my crush into a grandma. She still had to come to school. I liked her since first grade. She has no idea. She was 90 and she still had to take the math test. The teacher started calling her ma'am. She ran the mile in gym with a walker. She finished on Thursday. She fell asleep in every class and once in her suit. Then the bully called her grandma. She hit him with a purse. The next morning she looked a year younger. That night I figured it out. Every time she does something brave she gets a year younger. So I made her brave. I took her on the biggest rollercoaster in the state. 88. I signed her up to sing at the school assembly. 87. She told the lunch lady the meatloaf tasted like feet. 86. She skateboarded down the steepest hill in town. 85. At this rate she'd be young again in 70 years. So I did the bravest thing I've ever done. I asked her to the dance. She said yes and was young again in one second.

scripts.full_script: In my school, something walks between the desks every day at three. Everybody puts their head down and their thumb up. It walks up and down the rows, and presses one thumb. Whoever it presses is gone by morning. Whoever looks up is gone right then. And on the last day of school, it always presses one more. It only ever comes for the sixth grade. Nobody knows what it is. Not once, that's because of Nico. In kindergarten, every class practices. The teacher walks the rows, and you learn. Heads down, thumbs up, don't look, no matter what you hear. The first time, I was so scared, I almost looked. The boy at the next desk hooked his little finger around mine, under the desk. We never look, whatever we hear. Promise? And when it was over, he squeezed my finger and whispered, Okay, you can look. We've held fingers every day since. Nico is the funniest kid in school. He can make me laugh in the middle of a math test. Once, he made the whole class laugh so hard, the teacher had to leave the room. When it presses your thumb, it leaves a little white dot, like chalk. Mom's scrub all night. It never comes off. On the first day of sixth grade, the moms cried at the gate, and the dads held on too long. In September, there were 30 desks in my class, by Halloween, 22, by Christmas, 14. Every week, the janitor carried another desk out to the pile behind the school. By March, the pile was taller than the gym. Nico never cried about it. Not once. He'd just look at the empty desk and say, Better than you, that's just Nico. He always knew the exact second it was over. He said he could hear its feet stop. He always had chalk on his fingers. He was on board duty every single day. He volunteered, and some days, in the middle of it, his finger let go of mine for a minute. He said his hand got sweaty. In February, it pressed Mila's thumb. She didn't cry. She just stared at the white dot, and said the weirdest thing. It was warm, like a kid's finger. Everyone said she was just scared. The next morning, her chair was pushed in. Her backpack was still hanging on it. And at three the next day, there was one more white mark on its arm. By spring, six. Then one day in April, I felt it. Something brushed right past my thumb. I almost looked up. Nico's finger squeezed mine so hard it hurt. It pressed the kid behind me instead. That night, Nico walked me home. He didn't make one joke. At my door, he said, it's never going to pick you. I won't let it. And then it was the last day of school, one more three o'clock. Then we'd be in seventh grade, and it could never touch us again. Two desks left, mine and Nico's. The teacher didn't even look at us. Heads down, thumbs up, three o'clock. Its feet came down the aisle and stopped right between us. Nico's finger let go of mine. His chair scraped back. Then I heard him crying. And for the first time in my life, I looked up. Nico was standing in the aisle right next to it. Its long black hand was resting on his shoulder. The tip of his finger was white with chalk. It never picked anyone. Every day, it let Nico choose. As long as he never chose me. Mila, the kid behind me. Twenty-eight kids. For me. The way he did every day when it was over. Okay, you can look.

scripts.full_script: In my world, on our half of the planet, every wall is made of glass. Houses, schools, even bathrooms. Nobody here has a secret. If you dance in your pajamas, the whole street sees it. My neighbor sings in the shower. Badly. We all know the words now. Kids can't hide their report cards. Grandma can't hide her snacks. On the other half of the planet, it's the opposite. Every wall is thick stone. No windows. Nobody trusts anybody. Between us is the Great Wall. And there's one rule. Never cross it. The wall people will lock you in the dark forever, Dad says. Uncle Ray climbed it in 1999. We never saw him again. Our house is the last one before the Great Wall. And there's a tiny crack in it. The day I turned 12, a note slid through. Hi. I wrote back on my glass wall with a marker. Hi. Who are you? Mia, the next note said. For a year, we talked every day. She asked what the sun felt like. I asked what being alone felt like. She said it was quiet. She drew me the sun from what I told her. A yellow scribble. I kept it. Every night I fell asleep looking at the crack. She always knew things when I lost my first race, when I broke my arm. Lucky guess, she wrote. Sometimes she wrote, good job, before I even told her. And weird things happen here. Every glass house has a little red light in the corner. Smoke alarm, Dad says. Every week, a free box of crunchy-os shows up at our door. Dad always eats them right in front of the window. And whenever something big happens to me, I hear clapping from the other side of the wall. On my last birthday, the whole wall side set off fireworks. Coincidence, Mom said. Mia told me something else. Our king has a giant screen in his palace. It's always on. He laughs at it all day. Then my life started falling apart. Week one, our power went out. Only our house. Week two, a pipe burst and flooded my room. Week three, Dad lost his job. Mom cried in the kitchen. The whole street could see. Week four, our roof leaked right over my bed. And from over the wall, I heard people gasping. Every time something bad happened, the clapping got louder. Then a note slid through. They want you to cry, don't. Then Mia stopped writing. One day, five days, ten. So I did the one thing nobody ever does. I climbed the Great Wall. Mom screamed my name. Dad ran out in his socks. Halfway up, a stone broke under my foot. I hung on with one hand. My hands were bleeding. I reached the top. I jumped down into the dark and waited to be locked away. Nothing happened. Then I heard it. A thousand people breathing. Then I turned around. Every window on the wall side had a screen in it. And on every screen was me. The red lights were cameras. The crunchy-os were ads. My life was their number one TV show since the day I was born.

scripts.hook_0_to_3s: In this world, every kid has a little arrow over their head that points to their mom.
scripts.full_script: In this world, every kid has a little arrow over their head that points to their mom. And on Monday, mine pointed at my new teacher. You see, it never stops pointing, so no kid here has ever been lost. At the airport, 10,000 arrows spin around like crazy. At the Olympics, every runner's arrow points at the same row in the stands. On Mother's Day, every arrow in town points at the flower shop. Dads don't get one, they just follow the kids. There's only one way to break an arrow. Look your mom in the eye, say, you're not my mom, and mean it, then it fades. Take it back before it goes out, or you can never find her again. Nobody's ever been that dumb. Me? I've gotten a zero on every spelling test since first grade. And my mom walks every kid across Main Street, with a stop sign taller than me. She keeps a red marker in her pocket. Every sign in town that's spelled wrong, she fixes. School zone, fixed, 400 signs. Even my notes, she fixes them and draws a little smiley face. Then on Monday, we got a sub, Miss Tilly. Giant curly hair and a fancy British accent. Good morning, my darlings. And my arrow swung across the room and pointed right at her. Dexter yelled, Miss Tilly is his mom! Arrows don't break, so mine had to be the first. At recess, my arrow followed her around like a dog. At lunch, she ate a sandwich with the crusts cut off. Everybody chanted, Tilly Baby, Tilly Baby! After school, I ran to the crosswalk. There was mom with her stop sign, and my arrow pointed at her. See? Broken, one arrow, two moms, and one of them was British. On Tuesday, Dexter made a sign. Tilly Junior, then Miss Tilly bent down next to me. In front of everybody, all I could see was hair. Are you all right, love? And I yelled it. You're not my mom! I meant it. Miss Tilly stood up really slowly and walked out. My arrow flickered, then it started to fade. By the last bell, I could see through it. Then I found my spelling test, every word fixed in red marker. And a little smiley face. I stared at it. My arrow was never broken. Miss Tilly was mom. I ran outside. 3 o'clock, buses, cars, 200 kids. My arrow was blinking on, off. I couldn't tell which way it pointed. The crosswalk was empty, just the stop sign. Lying in the road. Then my arrow blinked one last time. Across the street, the bus stopped bench. A curly wig in her lap. But the cars weren't stopping. So I grabbed the stop sign and walked right into the street. Screech! Every car stopped. I looked her in the eye. You are my mom. Beep! My arrow lit up so bright, Dexter covered his eyes. Why didn't you tell me? Mom looked at the wig. I always wanted to be a teacher. So I fixed signs instead. Then your school finally said yes. And I thought you'd be embarrassed of me. Embarrassed? I got my first smiley face on a spelling test. Then on Wednesday, Dexter's arrows swung across the lunchroom. Straight to the new lunch lady. Hi, sweetie.

scripts.hook_0_to_3s: The monster ate my family, then it raised me. I was five. I've lived in its cave for
scripts.full_script: The monster ate my family, then it raised me. I was five. I've lived in its cave for seven years, and I still don't know why it didn't eat me, too. It's as big as a barn, with gray fur, three yellow eyes, and a mouth wide enough to swallow a horse. Every morning, it brings me breakfast, apples, fish. Once, a whole beehive. I think it's fattening me up. In winter, it curls around me like a blanket. When I fell through the ice on the river, it dove in after me. When wolves came, it chased them off the mountain, and when the hunter's horns blow, it hides me inside its mouth and closes its teeth like the bars of a cage until they're gone. Every night before I sleep, it touches its nose to my forehead. Then it walks to the mouth of the cave, looks down at the town, and makes a long, low sound that shakes the whole mountain. I've never known what it means. I remember the night it came. We lived in the last house before the woods. Mom pushed me under the bed. I heard the front door break. I heard dad shouting, and then I didn't. I heard mom scream my name, and then I didn't. Then three yellow eyes looked under the bed. It picked me up in its mouth gently, the way a cat carries a kitten, and it carried me up the mountain. I tried to run away three times. Every time it found me and carried me back. I hate it. I'm also all it has. Every winter, the hunters come up the mountain with torches and nets to get rid of it and bring me home. They're led by Mr. Garrick, the town hero. He's hunted monsters for 30 years. This winter, they found me first. I was fishing by the river and a net came down over my head. They carried me into town on their shoulders. People cried. They rang the church bell. The boy who survived the monster. Mr. Garrick took me into his own house. The biggest one in town gave me a warm bed and said you're safe now son. That night, I couldn't sleep. The bed was too soft, and the house was too quiet. I missed it, and I hated that I missed it, and then I heard it all the way from the mountain. That long, low sound. For seven years, I never knew what it meant. Now I did. It was calling me. It missed me too. The front door wasn't even locked. I ran up the mountain through the snow, faster than I'd ever run. Halfway up, I heard the horns behind me. Mr. Garrick was following my tracks. For seven years, he'd never found the cave. Tonight, I was leading him straight to it. At the cave, it was waiting. And for the first time, I was happy to see it. It opened its mouth to hide me, but the nets came down first. 20 hunters burst out of the trees and threw net after net over it. It roared and tore through them like paper, and hunters went flying into the snow. But Mr. Garrick just smiled. He dragged a sled out of the trees with three cages on it under a blanket, and he pulled the blanket off. Inside were three monsters, half its size, three yellow eyes each, so thin I could see their ribs. It stopped fighting. Mr. Garrick aimed his crossbow at the smallest one. Seven years ago, I stole these three from its nest. He said, people pay a fortune to see them. It came looking for them and found your house first. Thanks for showing me the way, son. It didn't eat me because we took its kids. A kid for a kid. That sound every night was never calling me. It was calling them. I crept to the sled and pulled the pins on all three cages. The babies ran to it, and it made a sound like laughing. It ate Mr. Garrick in one bite. The other hunters ran. It looked at me for a long time, touched its nose to my forehead one last time, and walked into the storm with its babies. The monster ate my family. Then it raised me. Tonight, I gave it back its family.

scripts.hook_0_to_3s: In this town, flowers are basically money farms. Every flower grows real money
scripts.full_script: In this town, flowers are basically money farms. Every flower grows real money instead of petals. And the rarer the flower, the more money it produces. Roses grow 100 dollar bills, and golden sunflowers can produce thousands of dollars every morning. Because of this, everyone owns a garden. Some families have entire farms filled with money flowers, while rich collectors spend millions buying rare seeds. But there's one flower nobody has successfully grown, the Diamond Lily. It's rumored to produce a million dollars every day. My family only had a tiny garden behind our apartment. We grew three daisies and one small rose, which barely gave us enough money to buy groceries. Meanwhile, our neighbor owned an enormous sunflower farm, and made more money in one week than my family earned in a year. One morning, I discovered a strange seed underneath our oldest flower pot. It was completely black, with a tiny golden symbol on it. I planted it immediately, hoping it would grow something valuable. The next morning, a tiny blue flower appeared. It didn't grow money. Instead, it produced a small silver key. I showed my dad, but he told me to throw it away. He said flowers sometimes produced unusual objects when their roots touched old pipes underground. But the following morning, the flower produced another key, and then another. I decided to investigate. I followed the roots beneath the garden, and discovered an old metal door hidden underneath our apartment building. The keys fit perfectly. Inside was a giant underground greenhouse filled with strange flowers. Some grew diamonds, others produced gold coins, and one enormous tree had hundreds of glowing seeds hanging from its branches. A note on the wall explained that this was the original money garden. Hundreds of years ago, every flower in town came from these seeds. But someone had stolen the rarest seeds and sold them to wealthy families, leaving ordinary people with only the cheapest varieties. Then, I heard footsteps. Our neighbor, the sunflower farmer, entered the greenhouse with several workers. He had been following me because he wanted to find the legendary seeds. He explained that he already owned most of the valuable flowers in town, but the original garden could make him richer than anyone alive. He offered to buy my black seed for an enormous amount of money. I refused, so he ordered his workers to grab it. I ran toward the glowing tree, and noticed something written on its trunk. The garden only grows when everyone can share. I suddenly understood why the rare flowers had stopped appearing. They weren't meant to belong to one person. Their seeds had to be planted across the town. I threw the black seed into the center of the greenhouse. They traveled through the pipes and appeared in gardens, parks, school yards, and empty fields. The next morning, strange flowers began growing everywhere. Families who had never owned valuable plants suddenly had golden roses and silver lilies. The sunflower farmer's private garden stopped producing money because the original garden had returned to the town. My family finally had enough money to move into a comfortable house. I even planted a small garden outside our new home. But one morning, I noticed something strange growing beside the flowers. A tiny black tree. It had no leaves, no petals, and no money. Instead, every branch was covered in little golden watches. And every watch was counting down.

scripts.full_script: If a royal guard smiles on duty, he loses his job forever. For a whole year, the princess has tried to make me smile. She tickled my face with a feather. I sneezed so hard, my hat flew off, but I didn't smile. She brought 40 puppies, one fell asleep on my boot, nothing. She sang in my ear, completely off key. Every pigeon in the palace left. She pretended to faint, I didn't move. She got up and called me rude. Soon, 3000 tourists came every day just to bet on when I cracked. Then one day, she didn't come. A week went by, then a month. The tourists stopped coming. I'd stood still for a year. It had never felt this long. Then one morning, the square was packed again. She stood right in front of me, closer than she'd ever been. She leaned in and whispered, you know why guards lose their job when they smile at me? Because they have to marry me. I smiled so wide, my face hurt. 3000 tourists screamed. She stepped back and grinned. Congratulations, you're fired.

scripts.full_script: The Halber steps over whole streets and takes whatever is exactly in the middle, the middle house, the middle seat, the middle child, so we do everything in even numbers. Last night, my brother was born. Now there are three of us. I'm the middle one. My sister, Philippa, is two years older. She still holds my hand on every street. Mom and Dad say, two kids and a baby. I counted three. They write him in the town book tomorrow. I haven't told anyone. Every table here has two chairs or four. We count before we sit. When a street counts one house too many, we build another. Nobody lives there. The church bell skips new. We go from eleven straight to one. The Halber counts houses with houses, kids with kids. When it takes a middle house, there's no gap. By morning, the two neighbors share a wall. Grandma's map puts our two seas a month apart. The middle of her map is blank. No one has ever seen the middle of the world. By breakfast, Philippa told the lady next door. The lady came back with her son. Borrow ours. She said. Then you're four. He sat next to me. He ate all my bread. He called my mom. Mom. At supper, his mother came back for him. Sorry. She said. Without him, we're three. Then my teacher knocked. A baby doesn't count until he walks. She said. Mom said. He's a whole baby. My teacher pinned a note on our door anyway. The note said. He can't walk yet. Then dad packed my bag. You'll sleep at your uncles tonight. He said. I got as far as the doorstep. Mom took the bag out of my hand. On the road, he's alone. She said. A kid alone is his own middle. At sunset, the ground shook twice. Two legs came down at both ends of our street. Our street has four houses. It can't take a house. So what did it come for? It bent down to our kitchen window. One long arm hangs from where its legs meet. It has no face. But it stopped at Philippa. Then me, then the baby. The baby counted. It was counting us. I didn't think. I ran out the front door. I left two kids inside. Two has no middle. The arms stayed at the window. Behind me, Philippa banged on the glass. Then the arm turned. I was alone on the street. I was my own middle. It came after me. Slow and low. I ran up hill to the bus stop. A woman stood there. I stood right next to her. Two. The arms stopped. I saw every house below pressed against the next. And I saw two seas at once. Grandma's map says they're a month apart. It doesn't want the middle. It wants the two sides to meet. Each time it takes a middle, the world gets shorter. No one has ever seen the middle of the world. It took that first. As long as I stayed in a pair, I was safe. Me and this stranger. I asked, can I stand here? As long as you like. She said, the arm hung above us. Then our front door opened. Philippa came running up the hill. Don't stand alone. She yelled. She grabbed my other hand. She was smiling. She thought she'd saved me. The bus came. She let it go. She was staying for me. I counted like we do before we sit. Three. Now the two legs are coming down. One on each side of us. Back in our kitchen. The baby is an only child. One child alone is a middle too. I'm the middle one again.

My crush is obsessed with the mask. Superhero. She has no idea it's me. Every night I save the city in a mask. I never say a word so nobody knows my voice. Every morning in class she sits next to me and talks about it. He's so brave. Not like you. You're scared of pigeons. It's true. Once a pigeon chased me out of the cafeteria and the whole school heard me scream. She covered her locker in his posters. She even made a board with every boy in school on it to find out which one was him. My photo had a big red X. Next to it, scared of pigeons. Then one night she climbed the clock tower and yelled for help just so he would show up. And then she slipped for real. I flew in and caught her. She was holding on to me, staring right into my eyes. Two inches away. Still no idea. Then a pigeon landed on my head. And I scream. The same scream from the cafeteria. She froze. See her? Then she gently shoot the pigeon away. You save the city. I'll save you from the pigeons.
